To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Dabbahu segment of the Afars rift, a nasent seafloor spreading center in continental lithosphere, ruptured in 2005 by 8 m, and that the magma intrusion that accompanied this event was the largest to occur on land in the satellite era, and that the magmatic intrusion was the main cause of the along-axis segmentation of the Afar Rift, and not normal faulting.
the Dabbahu segment of the Afan rift ruptured by 8 m in 2005, with most of the deformation caused by magma intrusion rather than seismic slip.

the Dabbahu magmatically segmented rift segment ruptured in 2005 and the entire segment was intruded by dykes, which were injected by magma from shallow magmatic chambers beneath Dabbhu and Gabho volcanos.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the initiation and evolution of continental rifts, and how they eventually evolve into oceanic spreading centres.
the role of magmatism in continental rupture and the initiation and maintenance of segmented magma supply to the nascent Afar seafloor spreading system.
the role of magmatism in continental rupture, which is the first stage in the formation of oceanic crust.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
magma intrusion, and not segmented normal faulting as has been previously thought, is what maintains and probably initiated along-axis segmentation in continental rifts.
the 2005 Dabbahu dyking episode was a continental version of the Krafla dyking episode.
magma injection via dyking maintains rift segmentation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
magma intrusion is the primary process that maintains and probably initiates the along-axis segmentation observed along this sector of Nubia– Arabia plate boundary.
the Afar segment of the Red Sea Rift is a nascent seismogenic spreading centre with a magma supply from a shallow magma chamber.
the Dabbahu segment is the largest segment to have ruptured on the African continent since 2002, when satellite geodesy became available.
The main takeaway from our work is that
magma intrusion is the dominant process of continental rupture, not normal faulting.

magmatism can be a major driver of continental rupture, and that magmatism and normal faulting can be decoupled in time, with magmatic segmentation occurring first, and then normal faults developing in response to magma withdrawal and/or lateral dyke propagation.
the Dabbahu segment is a magmatic segment, and that the magmatic segmentation is maintained by dyke intrusion, not by normal faulting.
